title: Why Binary Search Takes log n Steps

scenes.visual: Sixteen sorted cells; the middle cell glows gold and is compared with the target 41; the left half turns coral and fades; repeat until the target is green.

beats.text: Binary search looks for a target in a sorted array by checking the middle element first.
If the target is larger, the whole left half is discarded. If it is smaller, the right half goes. Either way, one comparison removes half the candidates.

scenes.visual: Bars n, n/2, n/4 ... shrink to 1 with a KaTeX formula n/2^k = 1 => k = log2 n; then a million vs 20 comparison.

beats.text: After k comparisons, only n over two to the k candidates remain. The search ends when that reaches one, so k is about log base two of n.
beats.say: After k comparisons, only n over two to the k candidates remain. The search ends when that reaches one, so k is about log base two of n.

beats.text: For a million elements that is just twenty comparisons, versus up to a million for a linear scan.
